metadata.title: Reading Isn't Reviewing.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: how do you build a risk-tiered verification checklist with Claude? Lands the carry-out that looks-right is not a review — a review is a checklist somebody can point to afterward.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B08 (the citation-at-strict checklist card: planted as a clean-reading fake that only 'open the source' catches; returned logged with timestamp and checkboxes as the reel closes)
metadata.one_flag: B07 - the checklist only replaces 'looks right' if every step stays genuinely checkable

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes that if Claude's answer looks right on a read-through, they've reviewed it. They haven't — they've only read it. So: what actually turns a read into a review?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'If Claude's answer looks right, I've reviewed it — right?', hesitates on 'reviewed', corrects to 'read'

props.text:
If Claude's answer
looks right, I've
reviewed it —
right?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('reviewed' -> 'read') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Claude can hand you a citation, a number, a chart, code, or a recommendation — and every one of those can be wrong in a way that reads perfectly clean. Deciding whether an answer is actually right takes more than reading it carefully.

shot.new_visual_element: five output-type cards (CITATION, NUMBER, CHART, CODE, REC) converging on one 'IS THIS RIGHT?' card

production_viz.label: Five outputs, one question
production_viz.mechanic: Five small pill cards in a row: CITATION, NUMBER, CHART, CODE, RECOMMENDATION. Arrows from each converge on a single card below reading 'IS THIS RIGHT?'. Caption beneath: 'reading it isn't reviewing it'.

beats.narration_text: That seems reasonable. If the wording is clean, the facts line up, and nothing looks out of place, a careful read feels like it should be enough — the same way a well-typed email doesn't need a second check.

shot.new_visual_element: a citation card, a magnifying glass passing over it, a checkmark forming

production_viz.label: The natural guess
production_viz.mechanic: A single citation card, formatted cleanly. A magnifying glass sweeps across it left to right. A confident checkmark forms beneath, captioned 'looks clean = reviewed?'.

beats.narration_text: Here's the case that breaks it: a fabricated citation, formatted exactly like a real one — right journal, right year, a title that sounds plausible. It reads perfectly clean. Opening the actual source is the only step that shows it doesn't exist.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - the citation card, checkmark forming, then cracking open to 'SOURCE: NOT FOUND'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - a clean-reading fake
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. The same citation card from B02: journal, year, title, all formatted correctly. A checkmark forms as before. Then the card cracks open like a shell to reveal, inside, terracotta text: 'SOURCE: NOT FOUND'. THIS EXACT CARD RETURNS AT B08.

beats.narration_text: The fix is a tool, not more careful reading: verification_gate.py takes an output type and a risk level as arguments, and prints back three to five concrete, checkable steps — not a feeling, a list.

shot.new_visual_element: INPUT (type + risk level) -> GEAR (the matrix) -> OUTPUT (checklist)

production_viz.label: A tool, not a feeling
production_viz.mechanic: Three boxes left to right: INPUT card reading 'output type + risk level', an arrow into a GEAR icon labeled 'verification_gate.py', an arrow out to an OUTPUT card reading '3-5 checkable steps'. Caption beneath: 'not a feeling — a list'.

beats.narration_text: The rules are specific to the combination. A citation always includes opening the actual source. A number at strict risk always includes an independent recalculation. A chart always gets its axis labels and its denominator checked. None of the six output types gets a generic checklist.

shot.new_visual_element: three-row table: CITATION -> open the source; NUMBER@strict -> recalculate; CHART -> axis + denominator

production_viz.label: Every combination has its own rule
production_viz.mechanic: A three-row table: CITATION -> 'OPEN THE SOURCE'; NUMBER @ STRICT -> 'INDEPENDENT RECALCULATION'; CHART -> 'AXIS LABELS + DENOMINATOR'. Caption beneath: 'none of the six is generic'.

beats.narration_text: Run it three times. Citation at strict: four steps, ending in open the source. Number at moderate: three steps — spot-check, denominator, units. Code at light: a two-step skim for obvious errors. Same tool, three genuinely different depths.

shot.new_visual_element: three terminal runs side by side, checklists of visibly different lengths

production_viz.label: Three genuinely different depths
production_viz.mechanic: Three narrow terminal-style cards side by side: CITATION/STRICT with four checkbox lines ending in 'open the source'; NUMBER/MODERATE with three lines (spot-check, denominator, units); CODE/LIGHT with two lines. Visibly different lengths, same header style.

beats.narration_text: One flag — this only replaces "looks right" if every step is genuinely checkable. A step that just says "seems plausible" has quietly turned back into the exact habit it was built to replace.

shot.new_visual_element: THE FLAG - a checklist step reading 'seems plausible (checked)', cracking open to reveal nothing was actually checked

production_viz.label: THE ONE FLAG - still checkable?
production_viz.mechanic: A single terracotta FLAG marker over the beat, the reel's only hedge, labeled as one. A checklist line reads 'seems plausible' with a checkbox ticked; it cracks open to reveal the box is empty behind it — nothing was actually checked.

beats.narration_text: Add a --log flag, and running the citation-at-strict case again writes out a markdown file — output type, risk level, timestamp, and each step with a checkbox, including open the source. That's the record, not just the answer. But finishing every checkbox doesn't prove the output was fully correct — the matrix catches known risks, not everything. And one failed step doesn't automatically mean it's wrong either — it means it needs a closer look.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - the citation card's checklist, now logged with timestamp and checkboxes; two dimmed captions beneath

production_viz.label: The record, then both directions
production_viz.mechanic: THE B03 ANCHOR RETURNS: the same citation card, now beside a markdown file card showing output type, risk level, an ISO timestamp, and four ticked checkboxes ending in 'open the source'. Beneath, two dimmed captions fade in: 'ALL CHECKS PASSED != FULLY CORRECT' and 'ONE FAILED STEP != WRONG'.

beats.narration_text: Looks right isn't a review. A review is a checklist somebody can point to afterward.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. I want to build a risk-tiered verification checklist for my own AI workflow — different verification depths matched to different levels of output risk. Help me design three tiers, list three to five concrete checkable steps for each output type at each tier, and flag any step that isn't specific enough to actually check. Liam, in for Bear.
